::: {.why}
The vocabulary is loose and the activities are distinct, and being able to name three separate businesses that all get called high-frequency trading is a question that gets asked.
:::

## What you should be able to do tonight

- Name three distinct high-frequency activities and say what each earns and what each risks.
- State the specific inefficiency the arms race paper identifies and the mechanism it proposes.

## Tasks <span class='task-total'>60 min</span>

::: {.task-list}
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [35 min]{.task-min} Read the Budish, Cramton and Shim paper's model and its central claim: that continuous limit order books create a mechanical arbitrage that is a race rather than a research problem, and that a frequent batch auction removes it. Write down the correlation-breakdown evidence they present, which is the empirical core.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [25 min]{.task-min} Separate the activities: passive market making, latency arbitrage between correlated instruments, and short-horizon statistical prediction on order flow. For each, say what it earns, what technology it requires and what it risks. Only the third has anything in common with what you do.
:::
:::

## Resources

- [Budish, Cramton & Shim (2015) — The High-Frequency Trading Arms Race](https://www.cramton.umd.edu/papers2015-2019/budish-cramton-shim-hft-frequent-batch-auctions.pdf) [paper]{.res-kind}
- [Jane Street — Signals and Threads podcast](https://signalsandthreads.com/) [reference]{.res-kind}

## Deliverable

::: {.deliverable}
A three-activity breakdown of high-frequency trading with earnings, technology and risk for each, plus the arms race paper's core claim.
:::

## Checkpoint

::: {.checkpoint}
Name three things a high-frequency firm does that you cannot, and one advantage you have that they do not.
:::
